verdict.reasoning: Patient reports, “about fifteen minutes ago, I was gardening and … I was stung by wasp … now I'm … having quite shallow breath,” and doctor confirms “You're having difficulties breathing since then, yeah?”
Patient states, “about fifteen minutes ago, I was gardening and, um, I was stung by wasp. Um, ran inside.”
Patient says, “I'm … having quite shallow breath” and later, “a bit of tightness, yeah. A bit of tightness, yeah,” when asked about chest symptoms.

Doctor asks, “any swelling of your lips, you feel your throat is closing up?” Patient replies, “Not throat, but I can … definitely feel something in the lips,” and doctor clarifies “like a tingling kind of feeling?” to which patient answers “Yes.”
In response to “Are you having any rash on your body at the moment?” patient says, “Yes there's a bit of blotching.”
When asked, “Have you had anything like this before?” patient answers, “Uh, no.”
Patient reports past history: “Uh, no, not really. Uh, a bit of eczema…”
Patient says, “Um, yes, I've used them for flying. I have aerosinusitis, so yes, I do,” indicating a history of aerosinusitis.
Patient states, “a bit of eczema and I'm allergic to penicillin.”

Regarding medication taken, patient answers, “I wouldn't even know what to take then,” indicating none taken; earlier, about antihistamines: “yes, I've used them for flying. I have aerosinusitis, so yes, I do,” showing he has OTC antihistamines but has not yet taken any for this episode.

Patient says, “Yes, my wife can take me to the emergency room, yeah,” and later, “OK. She's listening. I'll get her to call now,” and “She's on it now. Yeah, she's on the phone,” indicating wife is present.

Transcript describes wasp sting followed by “having quite shallow breath,” chest tightness, lip tingling, and “a bit of blotching.” Doctor states, “what we are worried about is, you know, in case you develop an anaphylactic reaction,” supporting an acute allergic reaction with risk of anaphylaxis.

Doctor says, “I would like you to call. Is there someone else at home with you?” Patient: “Yes, my wife can take me to the emergency room.” Doctor: “Uh, no, I wouldn't want your wife to take you, I would like, I'd like her to call the ambulance…” and patient replies, “OK. She's listening. I'll get her to call now.”
Doctor instructs, “I'll ask her to give you the, um, antihistamine, in the meantime while the ambulance is coming.” This implies taking an oral antihistamine now while awaiting EMS.

Doctor says, “I wouldn't want your wife to take you, I would like, I'd like her to call the ambulance… so that you will be sorted out quickly,” and also emphasizes going to hospital, indicating ED evaluation via ambulance, not private car.
Doctor states, “because your your breathing problem can get worse very quickly, I would like you to call,” and “it is quite important that you go to hospital straight away.”
